title: The format, the timer and the ballot
summary: Meet the shape of a formal debate, hand-rule the ballot you will be judged on, seal the season's final motion in an envelope for week 10, then deliver a first timed two minute opening speech on a motion you already know.
materials: paper, ruler and pencil for the ballot
an envelope and a card for the sealed motion

steps.title: What a formal debate actually is
steps.body:
Until now, a debate at this table meant an argument with good manners on top. This season it gets a shape, a clock and a ballot, and by week 12 you will run the whole thing in front of a judge who announces a result out loud.

Here is the shape. Two sides, called For and Against, and the speeches always come in the same order:

1. Opening speech, 2 minutes each side. This one builds your case and does nothing else. It is called the constructive, because it constructs.

2. Questions, 1 minute. Short questions, short answers, both sides asking.

3. Reply, 90 seconds each side. This one answers what the other side actually said.

4. Last word, 1 minute each side. One argument, the one you are winning, and everything spent on it.

Every week this season works on one of those four. This week is the opening speech, and only that.

The timer. The sand timer is not a punishment and it is not the enemy. It is the one thing both sides share: exactly the same sand, no matter who is talking, which is the only reason the whole thing is fair. A speech that runs long does not steal anybody's time but its own, because a judge stops writing at the bell and everything after it lands on the floor. Landing on time is a skill you can own, and it takes about six weeks of practice.

Clash. Two speeches that never touch each other are two speeches, not a debate. Clash is where the cases actually collide: they say the cost is too high, you say the cost is worth it, and now there is something for a judge to decide. If nobody in the room disagreed with anything you said, you did not argue, you presented.

The ballot. A judge does not vote for whoever was loudest, funniest or most confident. A judge writes down each side's main points, marks which ones got answered, and decides who won the argument that was actually had. Knowing what the judge is writing changes how you speak, which is why you are going to build a ballot before you ever speak into one.

The question of the week, running underneath all of it: why do people climb mountains when it is hard? Let it simmer while you work. Your recording ends with it.

Optional, and outside the hour: some weekend, watch a real middle school debate round together as a family, with popcorn and a blank ballot each. Compare ballots afterwards and argue about the result. It is not homework and nothing this season depends on it.

steps.title: Rule the ballot you will be judged on
steps.body:
Rule the ballot before you ever speak into one, because it tells you what a judge is listening for.

Take a sheet, landscape, and draw it out by hand:

Two wide columns, headed For and Against.

Three or four rows down the page, one per main point, so each side's point sits opposite the other side's.

A narrow column at the far right headed Answered? with a box per row, for ticking when somebody actually replied to that point rather than talking past it.

At the bottom, two lines: Decision, and Because. The second line is one sentence, and it has to name a specific argument, not a feeling.

Now use it once, small. Ask a grown-up to read out two short opposing statements, one sentence each, about anything at all. Fill in one row: their point on each side, and whether either statement actually answered the other. Most of the time it will turn out that they did not, and that is exactly the thing you are learning to notice.

Keep this sheet. Photocopy it or redraw it every week. It is the same paper the judge will be holding at the final.
checklist: My ballot has a column for each side and a row for each main point
There is a place to mark whether a point was actually answered
The bottom asks for a decision and one sentence naming why
I filled in one row from two statements I actually heard read aloud

steps.title: The sealed envelope
steps.body:
The season's last debate already has a motion. You are not allowed to know it.

Leave the room. A grown-up writes the motion on a card, puts it in an envelope and seals it. Come back, and write on the outside in your own handwriting: OPENS WEEK 10. Then it goes on a shelf where you will see it every single week between now and then.

Two reasons, and both matter. First, if you knew the motion now you would spend ten weeks quietly collecting arguments for the side you happen to like, and arrive at the final with half a brain warmed up. Second, at the final the sides are drawn on the day. Not chosen. Drawn. So when that envelope opens in week 10, you build both cases properly, because you will not find out which one you are defending until you are standing up.

Ten weeks of a sealed envelope on a shelf is a small kind of torture, and that is on purpose.
checklist: The envelope is sealed and I did not see what was written on the card
OPENS WEEK 10 is on the outside in my handwriting
It is standing somewhere I will see it every week

steps.title: The rematch: your first timed opening speech
steps.body:
Your first timed speech is a rematch. The motion is one you already argued last season: calculators should be allowed in every math test. You know this ground, which is the point. Today is not about finding ideas, it is about the shape and the clock.

Pick a side. Either one, and it does not have to be the one you picked last time.

Build the speech on paper first:

An opening line that says which side you are on and what you are going to prove. One sentence. A judge who hears nothing else should still know what you think.

Then three points. Each point is three things in a row: a claim, one sentence saying what is true; a reason, one or two sentences saying why it is true; and evidence, something from outside your own head. A number, a rule that actually exists, or something you have watched happen. Leave the evidence slot visible on the page so you can see whether you filled it or bluffed it.

Then a closing line that says, in different words from the opening, what you just proved.

Signposting: say my first point and my second point out loud, as words, in the speech. It feels clunky and it is not. A judge is writing while you talk, and the seams are what they write along.

Now deliver it. Two minute sand timer where you can see it, one take, no restarts. If you run dry early, stop and stand there: silence is better than filler, and a short speech that landed is stronger than a long one that wandered. If the sand runs out mid-sentence, stop mid-sentence. That is what the bell means.

Straight afterwards, still recording, say two things: whether you finished early, on time or got cut off, and what you would cut if you had to run it again 20 seconds shorter.

Then, last thing on the recording, answer the question of the week in your own words: why do people climb mountains when it is hard?
checklist: The first sentence says which side I am on and what I will prove
Three points, each with a claim, a reason and evidence from outside my own head
I said my first point and my second point out loud so the seams were audible
One take against the two minute sand, and I know whether I landed early, on time or got cut off
The recording ends with my own answer about why people climb

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: Record the two minute opening speech in one take with the sand timer in the frame, then the 20 seconds on what you would cut, then your answer to why people climb mountains when it is hard.
